title: Cognitive biases
examples: What is the difference between a bias and a stereotype?
Can I get rid of these cognitive biases?
Are these biases only for making decisions about people?

explain.say: Today we are learning about cognitive biases in your thinking.
First we look at confirmation bias in decision making.
For example you might only read news supporting your views.
Next we explore the anchoring effect in decision making.
Imagine a price starting at one hundred dollars for a jacket.
Finally we consider availability bias when remembering things.

faq.q: What is the difference between a bias and a prejudice?
faq.a: A bias is a systematic pattern of deviation in thinking. A prejudice is an unjustified negative attitude toward a group.
asks: Is it always bad to have a bias?

faq.q: Do these biases mean I am unintelligent?
faq.a: No, they are normal mental shortcuts our brains use. They are patterns of thinking, not measures of intelligence.
asks: Is this a sign of a weak mind?
Can I just stop thinking this way?

faq.q: How can I spot confirmation bias in my own thinking?
faq.a: Try actively seeking out reliable information that disagrees with your current beliefs. This forces a balanced view.
asks: What should I do when I feel strongly about something?
How do I check my own assumptions?

faq.q: Is anchoring always a problem in buying things?
faq.a: It can be, but it can also help set a reasonable starting point for negotiation. Context matters a lot.
asks: Does anchoring only happen with money?
Can I use anchoring to my advantage?

faq.q: If something is very recent, is it more likely to be available in my memory?
faq.a: Yes, highly emotional or very recent events tend to stick in our memory easily. This is the availability bias at work.
asks: Why do I remember dramatic things better?
Is emotional weight related to memory recall?

facts: Cognitive biases are systematic patterns of deviation from norm or rationality in judgment.
Confirmation bias leads people to favor information that confirms their existing beliefs.
The anchoring effect suggests that people rely too heavily on the first piece of information offered.
Availability bias makes us overestimate the likelihood of events that are easily recalled.

quiz.say: A student only reads articles that support their political opinions.
quiz.why: This shows seeking only information that confirms what you already think.

wrong.0: Overconfidence is about believing you know more than you actually do.
wrong.2: Anchoring relates to sticking to the first number you see, not the topic.
wrong.3: Availability bias is about how easily you can remember an event, not what you read.

quiz.say: When deciding on a car, you notice the first price quoted was very high, so you think any price is reasonable.
quiz.show: Bias: First price sets the range
quiz.why: The initial high price acts as an anchor, influencing your perception of fair value.

wrong.1: This is not about confirming a belief, but about judging value based on a starting point.
wrong.2: Availability bias relates to how easily you can recall past examples, not initial pricing.
wrong.3: Hindsight bias is believing an event was predictable after it has already happened.

quiz.say: After seeing a dramatic news report about a rare accident, you believe it happens much more often than it actually does.
quiz.why: The dramatic nature makes the event very easy to recall, leading to an overestimate of its frequency.

wrong.0: This is about recall frequency, not confirming a belief about the event.
wrong.1: Anchoring requires a specific starting number or piece of information to fix your judgment.
wrong.2: The framing effect relates to how the information is presented, not just how easily it is remembered.
